title: CSC3710 2026-09-01 — Recursive Definitions: Strings, ℕ and Addition

questions.q: According to the textbook view in lecture, the theoretical foundations of computer science draw on which disciplines?
questions.explain: The slide lists logic (correct reasoning, proofs), electrical engineering (circuits), brain research (McCulloch–Pitts neurons, which led to finite automata) and linguistics (grammars, formal languages). Economics is not on the list. The lecture also noted the list is dated: quantum computing now draws on quantum mechanics too.

questions.q: Why was linguistics, and Noam Chomsky in particular, called "a big part of our course"?
choices: Chomsky's classification of grammars (the Chomsky hierarchy) organizes the languages and machines the course studies
The course studies natural-language translation software
Linguistics supplies the Boolean algebra used in circuits
questions.explain: Chomsky (1956) classified grammars into four nested types — regular, context-free, context-sensitive, recursively enumerable — each matched to a machine (finite automaton, pushdown automaton, linear-bounded automaton, Turing machine). Much of the course follows this hierarchy, and a *language* here is just a set of strings.

questions.q: In the Chomsky hierarchy, which machine recognizes the **regular** languages (type 3)?
questions.explain: Type 3 (regular) ↔ finite automata, like the vending-machine DFA. Context-free ↔ pushdown automata, context-sensitive ↔ linear-bounded automata, recursively enumerable ↔ Turing machines.

questions.q: In this course, a recursive definition of a set of strings over {a, b} is already a definition of a *language*.
questions.explain: A language is simply a set of strings, so every recursively defined string set in the lecture (even-length strings, odd number of a's, …) is a language.

questions.topic: Theory uses only its own definitions
questions.q: The textbook principle says theorems and proofs in a theory may use only the definitions of the theory's concepts. What does this require?
choices: Precise definitions of both the objects of the domain and the operations on them
A list of the first few elements of every set, followed by "…"
Use of commutativity and other familiar arithmetic facts
questions.explain: If proofs can use only definitions, then both the **objects** (here ℕ, built from 0 and s) and the **operations** (here addition) must be defined precisely. Familiar facts such as commutativity cannot be assumed; they must be proven from those definitions.

questions.q: "We are at the beginning of the world." Under this view, which of the following exists and may be used when working with ℕ in this lecture?
choices: The fact that m + n = n + m
questions.explain: Only 0 and s exist at the start. 5 is only a name for s(s(s(s(s(0))))), multiplication has not been defined, and commutativity is a theorem that has not been proven yet — none of those may be used as given.

questions.q: Writing ℕ = {0, 1, 2, 3, …} counts as a precise definition of ℕ.
questions.explain: The three dots make the reader guess the pattern, and a pattern can be continued in more than one way. A recursive definition replaces the "…" with an exact recipe. That is why the instructor erased the trailing dots from the list of strings with an odd number of a's.

questions.q: What are the three parts of a recursive definition?
questions.explain: Basis: finitely many elements put in directly. Recursive step: operations that build new elements from existing ones (a recipe). Closure: nothing else belongs — only what the basis and finitely many rule applications produce.

questions.q: Why do we need recursive definitions at all?
choices: To define sets with infinitely many elements precisely
To define finite sets more compactly than listing them
questions.explain: A finite set can simply be listed. Recursive definitions exist so that **infinite** sets can be defined precisely, without resorting to an imprecise "…".

questions.q: What goes wrong if a recursive definition leaves out the closure clause?
choices: Nothing rules out extra elements, so the set is not pinned down — anything could also be in it
No elements can be generated from the basis
The recursive step can no longer be applied
questions.explain: The basis and rules only say what *is* in the set. Without closure ("nothing else"), a string with the wrong property could also be in the set without contradicting anything. Closure makes the set **exactly** what the recipe generates.

questions.q: Which is the recursive definition of ℕ used in the course?
choices: Basis: 0 ∈ ℕ. Step: if n ∈ ℕ then s(n) ∈ ℕ. Closure: only 0 and what is obtained from 0 by finitely many applications of s.
Basis: 1 ∈ ℕ. Step: if n ∈ ℕ then s(n) ∈ ℕ. Closure: nothing else.
Basis: 0 ∈ ℕ. Step: if n ∈ ℕ then n + n ∈ ℕ. Closure: nothing else.
questions.explain: In this course 0 is a natural number, so 0 is the basis, and the successor s generates the rest. Starting at 1 omits 0; using n + n from 0 only ever gives 0 (and uses an undefined operation); and the listing with "…" is not a definition.

questions.q: In this course, 0 ∈ ℕ.
questions.explain: The course uses ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …}; 0 is the basis of the recursive definition of ℕ.

questions.q: The closure clause of ℕ says elements are obtained from 0 by a **finite** number of applications of s. What would "infinitely many" allow that we do not want?
choices: An "infinite" object like s(s(s(…))) that is not any natural number
Only finitely many natural numbers would exist
Nothing — finite and infinite give the same set
questions.explain: Every natural number is sᵏ(0) for some finite k. The set ℕ is infinite, but each element is reached in finitely many steps; allowing infinite chains would admit objects that are not natural numbers. (The transcript's "infinity many" was a mishearing.)

questions.q: Write s³(0) in full using nested s's and parentheses.
questions.explain: sᵏ(0) means s applied k times to 0, so s³(0) = s(s(s(0))), also written sss0. Its number name is 3, but number names are only for checking.

questions.q: In a recursive definition, the basis may contain infinitely many elements.
questions.explain: The basis designates a **finite** number of elements. If you could put infinitely many elements in the basis you would need another way to describe them — which is the problem recursive definitions solve.

questions.q: What is the course's standard method ("we will always do it like this") for checking a recursive definition of a set of strings?
choices: Describe the target set S in words, define K recursively, generate K's shortest elements, argue whether S = K
Define K, prove K is infinite, then list S alphabetically
List S up to length 3 and add "…"
Write a regular expression, then convert it to a DFA
questions.explain: Pink rectangle: describe S. Blue rectangle: define K. Then generate the shortest elements of K and compare against S. A real proof of S = K would use structural induction.

questions.q: Why does the method name the defined set K instead of reusing S?
choices: The description and the definition are different objects, and the claim to check is S = K
K is always a subset of S
S is reserved for the successor function
It makes no difference; it is only style
questions.explain: S is described in words; K is built by rules. They are separate objects that might or might not coincide. If both were called S, the claim "S = K" would look trivially true and there would be nothing to check.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid counterexample showing a recursive definition K does **not** define the described set S?
choices: A string K generates that is not in S
A string in S that K cannot generate
A string in both S and K
A string in neither S nor K
questions.explain: A counterexample shows K is too big (it generates something outside S) or too small (it misses something in S). A string in both, or in neither, is consistent with S = K and proves nothing.

questions.q: To show a recursive definition is wrong, you need a full structural-induction proof.
questions.explain: Showing a definition is **wrong** is easy: one counterexample suffices, no proof needed. It is showing a definition is **right** that needs structural induction.

questions.q: If a program shows K and S agree on all strings up to length 10, that proves K = S.
questions.explain: Agreement up to some length is evidence, not proof — a difference could appear at length 11. A *disagreement*, however, is a genuine counterexample.

questions.q: Which statements about generating elements of a recursively defined set are correct?
choices: Elements may be listed in any order
The same string produced twice by different rules is not an error
t·a and ta mean the same thing
questions.explain: Sets are unordered, so any order is fine (shortest-first is just practical). Repetitions are harmless. The dot is concatenation and may be omitted. |λ| = 0 and 0 is even, so λ has even length. Alphabetical order is not required.

questions.q: The other section proposed: basis λ ∈ K; if t ∈ K then t·t·a ∈ K and t·t·b ∈ K. Why is this wrong as a definition of the even-length strings?
choices: With t = λ it generates a, which has odd length
It generates aa, which has odd length
It is correct; nothing is wrong
questions.explain: λ is the only element at first, so t = λ gives λ·λ·a = a. |a| = 1 is odd, so K generates a string outside V. That single counterexample settles it.

questions.q: In the definition basis λ; rules t·t·a and t·t·b, each rule maps a string of length n to one of length 2n + 1. Starting from λ (length 0), what is the length of the strings produced at the **third** execution of the recursive step (lengths go 0 → 1 → 3 → ?)
questions.explain: 2·3 + 1 = 7. The lengths in K are 0, 1, 3, 7, 15, … = 2ᵏ − 1, so apart from λ every string in K has odd length — the definition generates almost none of the right strings.

questions.q: Writing the generated string as λ·λ·a instead of a is incorrect.
questions.explain: λ can be inserted into a concatenation any number of times without changing the string, so λ·λ·a = a. There is no built-in notion of "simplification" in the theory — just as 2 + 2 is a correct answer to "3 + 1".

questions.q: Basis λ ∈ K; if t ∈ K then t·a·b ∈ K and t·b ∈ K. Is K the set of even-length strings over {a, b}?
choices: No — t = λ gives b, which has odd length
Yes — each rule adds an even number of symbols
Yes — it generates ab and b, covering both letters
questions.explain: λ·b = b has length 1, so K contains an odd-length string. (It also fails the other way: aa is never generated, since every non-λ string ends in b.)

questions.q: What is the shortest string of even length over {a, b}?
questions.explain: |λ| = 0, and 0 is even, so λ is the shortest even-length string and belongs in the basis.

questions.q: Which definition generates exactly the even-length strings over {a, b}?
choices: Basis λ; if t ∈ K then t·aa, t·ab, t·ba, t·bb ∈ K
Basis a, b; if t ∈ K then t·aa, t·ab, t·ba, t·bb ∈ K
Basis λ; if t ∈ K then t·a, t·b ∈ K
Basis aa; if t ∈ K then t·aa ∈ K
questions.explain: Starting at λ and appending any two-symbol block keeps length even and reaches every even-length string. Basis a, b gives the odd-length strings; t·a, t·b gives all strings; basis aa with t·aa only gives a²,a⁴,… (and misses λ).

questions.q: How many strings of length 4 are there over {a, b}?
questions.explain: Each of the 4 positions has 2 choices: 2⁴ = 16. Rules 1–4 applied to the four length-2 strings give 4 × 4 = 16 strings, so none is missing — the "orange rectangle" argument.

questions.q: The odd-length strings were defined with the same four rules (t·aa, t·ab, t·ba, t·bb). What changed?
choices: Only the basis: a and b instead of λ
The rules prepend instead of append
Nothing; the sets are the same
questions.explain: Adding two symbols preserves parity, so the basis decides it: λ (length 0) gives even lengths, a and b (length 1) give odd lengths. Rules applied to a, b give all 8 length-3 strings.

questions.q: In lecture, Rules 5 (t·aaaa) and 6 (a·t·aaa) of the even-length definition were **proven** redundant.
questions.explain: The word was "**seem**": they appeared to add nothing, but nothing was proven in class. (The lesson's enrichment proof does show they are redundant: Rules 1–4 already produce every even-length string, and Rules 5–6 produce only even-length strings.)

questions.q: What makes a rule *redundant* in a recursive definition?
choices: It is correct but only produces strings the other rules already produce
It produces strings outside the target set
It is applied to the basis only
questions.explain: A redundant rule is harmless — it never generates a wrong string — but removing it does not change the defined set. A rule that produces wrong strings is not redundant; it is incorrect.

questions.q: Why does every even-length string w with |w| ≥ 2 get generated by Rules 1–4 (t·aa, t·ab, t·ba, t·bb)?
choices: w = t·xy where xy are its last two symbols and t is shorter and even-length, so by induction t ∈ K and one rule appends xy
Because every even-length string starts with a
questions.explain: Induction on length: λ is the basis; any longer even-length string splits into an even-length prefix t plus a final pair xy ∈ {aa, ab, ba, bb}, and the matching rule builds it from t.

questions.q: Applying t·aa, t·ab, t·ba, t·bb to the basis {a, b} produces how many distinct strings of length 3?
questions.explain: 2 choices of t × 4 rules = 8, and there are exactly 2³ = 8 strings of length 3, so every length-3 string is generated.

questions.q: Which is the recursive definition of addition on ℕ?
choices: m + 0 = m;  m + s(n) = s(m + n)
0 + m = m;  s(m) + n = m + n
m + 1 = s(m);  m + n = n + m
questions.explain: Basis: adding 0 gives the same number. Recursive step: adding the successor of n gives the successor of m + n. It only ever handles an s on the **right** argument, and uses only 0 and s.

questions.q: What does each application of the recursive step m + s(n) = s(m + n) do?
choices: Peels one s off the second argument and moves it outside
Peels one s off the first argument
questions.explain: The outer s of the right argument moves outside the sum. Repeat until the right argument is 0, then the basis m + 0 = m finishes.

questions.q: In s(s(s(s(0)))) + s(s(0)), applying the recursive step once gives:
questions.explain: Match the second argument s(s(0)) to s(n) with n = s(0). Then m + s(n) = s(m + n) = s( s(s(s(s(0)))) + s(0) ). The fully computed answer (option 4) takes one more step and the basis.

questions.q: Computing s(s(s(0))) + s(s(s(s(s(0))))) using only the definition (without swapping), how many applications of the **recursive step** are needed before the basis applies?
questions.explain: Each step peels one s off the second argument, which has five s's. After 5 steps you reach s⁵(sss0 + 0), and the basis gives s⁸(0).

questions.q: How many s's are in the final result of s(s(s(0))) + s(s(s(s(s(0)))))?
questions.explain: The result is s(s(s(s(s(sss0))))) = s⁸(0). Number names are only for checking: 3 + 5 = 8.

questions.q: Using only the definition, s(s(0)) + s(s(s(0))) equals:
choices: s(s(0)) + s(s(s(0))) cannot be computed without commutativity
questions.explain: Three recursive steps: s(ss0 + ss0) → s(s(ss0 + s0)) → s(s(s(ss0 + 0))) → basis → s(s(s(ss0))) = s⁵(0). No commutativity is needed; the definition works for any order of arguments.

questions.q: How do you know an addition computation built from the definition is finished?
choices: The expression contains no "+", so it is a natural number sᵏ(0)
The second argument has one s left
You have applied the recursive step exactly twice
questions.explain: Once the basis m + 0 = m removes the last "+", what remains is a string of s's around 0 — a natural number — and nothing more can be applied.

questions.q: It is fine to replace s(s(s(0))) by 3 in the middle of a computation to speed it up.
questions.explain: Number names "are not in this world"; only 0 and s exist. Use names like 3 only to **check** your answer at the end.

questions.q: The instructor said the definition of addition is "like an implementation of addition". Which programming idea does it mirror?
choices: A recursive function: base case n = 0 returns m, otherwise return s(add(m, n − 1))
A for-loop over the first argument
A lookup table of all sums
questions.explain: The basis is the base case, and the recursive step is the recursive call on a smaller second argument; the result is assembled on the way back, one s per call.

questions.q: A recursive definition of multiplication (m · 0 = 0; m · s(n) = (m · n) + m) illustrates what about how theories are built?
choices: New operations are defined using ones already defined — here, addition
Multiplication must be taken as an axiom
Addition is defined in terms of multiplication
questions.explain: Multiplication's recursive step uses +, which is already defined. Theories grow by defining new concepts from existing ones. (Here "·" means numeric multiplication, not concatenation.)

questions.q: Using the definition, how many s's are in s(s(0)) + 0?
questions.explain: Directly by the basis m + 0 = m: s(s(0)) + 0 = s(s(0)). No recursive step is needed.

questions.q: A student wanted to compute 3 + 5 as 5 + 3 to peel fewer s's. Why is that not allowed for free?
choices: Swapping uses commutativity, which must be stated and proven from the definitions first
The definition forbids the first argument from being larger
questions.explain: Addition *is* commutative, but in a theory built from only 0 and s, m + n = n + m is a **theorem**. The definition only handles an s on the right, so you must prove commutativity before using it.

questions.q: In the theory built from 0, s and the definition of addition, m + n = n + m is one of the given definitions.
questions.explain: It is not given; it has to be proven by induction, using two lemmas: 0 + n = n and s(m) + n = s(m + n).

questions.q: Which lemmas are used in the standard proof that m + n = n + m?
questions.explain: Lemma 1 (0 + n = n) handles the base case, and Lemma 2 (s(m) + n = s(m + n)) handles the step: m + s(n) = s(m + n) = s(n + m) = s(n) + m. The other two are false.

questions.q: What is structural induction?
choices: Proving a property holds for every element of a recursively defined set by checking the basis and showing every rule preserves it
Listing elements until a pattern appears
Induction on the number of rules
questions.explain: It is "a version of mathematical induction for sets": the basis elements have the property, each rule turns elements with the property into elements with the property, and closure says nothing else is in the set.

questions.q: To prove S = K for a recursively defined K, you show two directions. Which is **soundness**?
choices: K ⊆ S — the definition generates nothing wrong
S ⊆ K — the definition misses nothing
questions.explain: Soundness (K ⊆ S) is usually by structural induction on K's rules. Completeness (S ⊆ K) is usually by induction on string length: show every string in S can be built.

questions.topic: Induction on n is valid because…
questions.q: Proofs about all natural numbers by induction on n (prove for 0, then from n to s(n)) are valid because of which part of ℕ's definition?
choices: The closure clause: every natural number is reached from 0 by finitely many s's
questions.explain: If the claim holds for 0 and passes from n to s(n), it holds for everything reachable from 0 in finitely many steps — and closure says that is all of ℕ.

questions.q: For the five-rule odd-number-of-a's definition, which invariant does the soundness proof show every rule preserves?
choices: The number of a's is odd
The number of b's is even
questions.explain: t·b and b·t leave #a unchanged; t·aa, a·t·a, a·a·t add 2. Either way an odd count stays odd, and the basis a has one a.

questions.q: Which strings over {a, b} have an odd number of a's?
questions.explain: a, ab, abb, bab each have one a. aa has two, λ has zero (0 is even), baba has two. Students in class first forgot abb and bab.

questions.q: How many strings of length 4 over {a, b} have an odd number of a's?
questions.explain: Exactly half of all 2⁴ = 16 strings: C(4,1) + C(4,3) = 4 + 4 = 8. In general the count is 2ⁿ⁻¹.

questions.q: Why must a be in the basis of any recursive definition of the strings with an odd number of a's (using concatenation rules)?
choices: a is the shortest element, and concatenation only makes strings longer, so no rule could produce it
The basis must always contain every single symbol
Because λ has an odd number of a's
questions.explain: Rules built from concatenation always produce strings at least as long as t (usually longer). The shortest element can never be the output of a rule, so it must be put in directly.

questions.q: Why was the proposed rule t·a ∈ K rejected?
choices: With t = a it gives aa, which has an even number of a's
questions.explain: Appending one a flips parity, so from a it produces aa — outside the target set. One incorrect string is enough to reject a rule.

questions.q: Why is t·aa ∈ K an acceptable rule?
choices: Adding two a's changes the count by 2, so an odd count stays odd
It generates every string in S
It is the only rule needed
questions.explain: Parity is preserved by adding an even number of a's. The rule is **sound**; whether the rules together are **complete** is a separate question.

questions.q: Assuming t has an odd number of a's, which rules always produce a string that also has an odd number of a's?
questions.explain: Adding b's changes nothing and adding two a's keeps parity. t·a and a·t add one a and flip parity, producing strings outside S.

questions.q: Basis a; rules t·b, t·aa, b·t. What does the first execution of the recursive step produce?
questions.explain: Only t = a is available: a·b = ab, a·aa = aaa, b·a = ba.

questions.topic: Second execution, t = ab and ba
questions.q: Basis a; rules t·b, t·aa, b·t. Which strings come from t = ab or t = ba in the second execution?
questions.explain: t = ab: abb, abaa, bab. t = ba: bab, baaa, bba. bab appears twice — repetitions are fine. aab has two a's and cannot appear.

questions.q: With basis a and rules t·b, t·aa, b·t, why can ababa never be generated?
choices: Every generated string other than a ends in b, ends in aa, or starts with b — ababa does none of these
ababa has an even number of a's
The rules can generate it; it just takes many steps
questions.explain: ababa has three a's, so it is in S, but it starts with a and ends in ba, matching no rule's output shape. That makes it a counterexample: K is too small.

questions.q: With basis a and rules t·b, t·aa, b·t, what is the **shortest** string with an odd number of a's that cannot be generated? (length 4)
questions.explain: aaba has three a's, starts with a and ends in ba — the same shape argument as ababa, one symbol shorter. A program confirms it is the shortest missing string.

questions.q: Which added rule produces ababa from t = bab?
questions.explain: a·bab·a = ababa. a·t·a adds two a's, so it is sound, and it fills the "starts and ends with a" gap.

questions.q: Adding t·aba to rules t·b, t·aa, b·t still misses a string. Which one?
questions.explain: aabba has three a's, starts with a and ends in bba; none of t·b, t·aa, b·t, t·aba can produce that ending. ababa = ab·aba *is* produced; abb and bab were already produced.

questions.q: The student's claim that t·b, b·t, a·t·a alone (with basis a) define exactly the strings with an odd number of a's is correct.
questions.explain: Completeness: a string w in S ending in b is t·b; starting with b is b·t; otherwise it starts and ends with a, so w = a·u·a with u having an odd number of a's (since #a(w) ≥ 3). Induction on length finishes it. So Rules 2 and 5 are redundant.

questions.q: In the completeness proof for rules t·b, b·t, a·t·a, a string w ∈ S of length ≥ 2 that neither starts nor ends with b is written w = a·u·a. Why does u have an odd number of a's?
choices: #a(w) is odd and at least 3, so #a(u) = #a(w) − 2 is odd
Every substring of w has an odd number of a's
questions.explain: w starts and ends with a, so #a(w) ≥ 2; odd means ≥ 3. Removing two a's keeps parity odd, so u ∈ S, u is shorter, and by induction u ∈ K; then a·t·a builds w.

questions.q: Basis a ∈ K, b ∈ K; if t ∈ K then t·t·t ∈ K. Which set is K?
choices: {a^(3ᵏ), b^(3ᵏ) : k ≥ 0} — a single repeated letter, length a power of 3
All strings over {a, b} whose length is a multiple of 3
questions.explain: Each application triples the length, and since t has one value within the rule, a's and b's never mix: a, aaa, a⁹, a²⁷, … and b, bbb, b⁹, …

questions.q: From basis {a, b} with rule t·t·t, the string aba can be generated by choosing t = a, t = b, t = a for the three copies.
questions.explain: A variable has **one value within a rule**: all three t's are the same string. So t·t·t never mixes letters, and aba is not generated.

questions.q: Which rule, with basis {a, b}, generates every nonempty string over {a, b}?
choices: If t ∈ K and w ∈ K, then t·w ∈ K
If t ∈ K, then t·t ∈ K
If t ∈ K, then t·t·t ∈ K
If t ∈ K, then a·t·a ∈ K
questions.explain: Two different variables can take different values (t = a, w = b gives ab), so any nonempty string can be assembled. The single-variable rules only repeat one string.

questions.q: In the t·t·t definition, what is the length of the string produced from t = a⁹?
questions.explain: a⁹·a⁹·a⁹ = a²⁷: each application triples the length, giving lengths 1, 3, 9, 27, …

questions.q: Basis b ∈ K; if t ∈ K then t·t ∈ K. Which set is K?
questions.explain: Doubling from length 1 gives lengths 1, 2, 4, 8, …, powers of 2. b³ is never produced, so it is not all strings of b's; and b itself has odd length.

questions.q: What does b⁹ mean in this course?
choices: b multiplied by itself nine times
The ninth symbol of the alphabet
questions.explain: Exponent notation is repetition by concatenation. "We are not in the world of numbers", so do not read it as a numeric power.

questions.q: What string does a⁰ denote? (give its symbol)
questions.explain: Zero copies of a concatenated is the empty string λ (some books write ε).

questions.q: aaa aaa aaa written with spaces denotes three separate strings.
questions.explain: The spaces (or dots) only show the pattern. Everything is concatenation, so it is one string, a⁹.

questions.q: Basis a, b; rule t·t·t. Which strings are in K?
questions.explain: Lengths must be powers of 3 with a single letter: a (1), bbb (3), a⁹ (9), b²⁷ (27). aaaaaa has length 6, not a power of 3; ab mixes letters.

questions.q: Which statements about strings are true?
choices: In this course, a·b means a multiplied by b
questions.explain: λ is the identity for concatenation and has length 0. The dot means concatenation, not multiplication. Σ\* is all strings over Σ, including λ.

questions.q: Which recursive definition gives exactly the strings over {a, b} that **start with a**?
choices: Basis a; if t ∈ K then t·a ∈ K and t·b ∈ K
Basis a; if t ∈ K then a·t ∈ K and b·t ∈ K
Basis λ; if t ∈ K then a·t ∈ K
Basis a, b; if t ∈ K then t·a ∈ K
questions.explain: Appending never changes the first symbol, and any string starting with a can be built from a by appending its remaining symbols. Prepending b (option 2) would produce ba; option 3 gives only a's (plus λ); option 4 includes b.
